item.title: U.S. futures point higher led by rebound for Nvidia
item.description: Tech stocks are leading U.S. futures higher Wednesday after Nvidia easily exceeded Wall Street expectations as it deals with the abrupt departure of CEO Jensen Huang.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — A fifth straight drop for the S&P 500 on Wednesday dragged Wall Street to its longest losing streak since June, as Nvidia and other stocks tied to artificial intelligence technology kept swinging on uncertainty about how much strength is left in the AI boom. The S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent after zigzagging between gains and losses through the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 561 points, or 1.1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite added 0.4 per cent. Nvidia once again was at the centre of the market’s moves. Its stock initially jumped 2.7 per cent after the chip company reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Perhaps more importantly, it also gave a forecast for revenue in the current quarter that was better than expected. But the stock quickly erased all its gain and then finished with a loss of 2.9 per cent. The question is whether Nvidia’s big growth can continue despite the turmoil created by the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. He had an immense personality that drew attention and investment to AI, and he built Nvidia into a company so big that it helped to fund some of the industry’s growth itself. “Our momentum is real,” Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, told investors and financial analysts after announcing the company’s latest results. “Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us. And employees are committed. We’ve got this.” The encouraging numbers and words coming from Nvidia, though, failed to create lasting gains for the price of its stock or for others across the industry. Micron Technology, whose sales of memory chips exploded with the AI boom, went from an early rise of 1.5 per cent to a drop of 1 per cent. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents access to them out to customers over the cloud, sank 4.1 per cent and has lost nearly a third of its value so far this year. The entire industry has been swinging recently. Besides criticism that AI stock prices simply shot too high in their frenzy, the industry is facing worries that this month’s sweeping victories for Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections could mean more regulation for it. Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks of oil companies were heavy weights due to drops for oil prices. ExxonMobil fell four per cent, and Chevron sank 4 per cent after the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 1.3 per cent to settle at US$91.95. The drop in oil prices helped to pull yields down in the bond market, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury eased to 5.06 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Tuesday. High yields have made mortgages more expensive to get, which has chilled the housing industry. But they’ve moderated over the last month, and a report on Wednesday said homebuilders broke ground on more projects last month than economists expected. That helped push stocks of homebuilders modestly higher, and Lennar added 0.7 per cent. Some of the strongest gains on Wall Street came from retailers following their profit reports. TJX rallied 8 per cent after the company behind the TJ Maxx and Marshalls stores reported slightly better earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Ernie Herrman said he expects momentum to accelerate through the holiday shopping season. Target climbed four per cent following a better-than-expected profit report, which included its strongest quarterly sales gain in roughly five years. Take-Two Interactive Software revved 6.2 per cent higher amid glowing reviews for its latest “Grand Theft Auto” video game. All told, the S&P 500 fell 16.90 points to 7,323.63. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 561.25 to 50,198.17, and the Nasdaq composite rose 101.50 to 24,429.88. In stock markets abroad, indexes fell in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. London’s FTSE 100 sank 1.3 per cent after a report said inflation in the United Kingdom worsened. That could up the pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates to get inflation under control. Expectations are high that the Federal Reserve in Washington will raise its own interest rate when it meets next month, after it made no move last month. Notes released Wednesday from the Fed’s latest meeting indicated some officials are considering a larger increase to rates than usual in December. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 2 per cent a day after dropping to its lowest closing level since February. It’s swung in particular because its market is dominated by two stocks tied to the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Writer Elaine Lai contributed to this report.

item.title: S&P/TSX composite down nearly 750 points, oil and gold also tumble
item.description: Canada’s main stock index was down more than 650 points, weighed down by losses in the heavyweight mining, energy and financial stocks.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index fell nearly 750 points Wednesday, weighed down by losses in the heavyweight mining, energy and financial stocks, while the prices of oil and gold also fell.   The S&P/TSX composite index was down 737.25 points at 34,578.05. In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 561.25 points at 50,198.17. The S&P 500 index was down 16.90 points at 7,323.63, while the Nasdaq composite was up 101.50 points at 24,429.89.   The Canadian dollar traded for 69.80 cents US compared with 69.97 cents US on Tuesday. The January crude oil contract was down US$2.34 at US$82.31 per barrel.     The December gold contract was down US$122.30 at US$3,741.90 an ounce.   --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

item.title: Alberta government to require cleanup funds to be set aside for each new well drilled
item.description: The Alberta government has introduced legislation that would require oil and gas companies to set aside funds for the future cleanup of every new well drilled.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: The Alberta government has introduced legislation that would require oil and gas companies to set aside funds for the future cleanup of every new well drilled. If passed, the bill would create the Resource Asset Closure Assurance and Stewardship Fund. Money would follow each well through its life cycle, even if ownership changes hands. Companies would be required to make an initial payment of up to $50,000 followed by equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The new rules are expected to apply to wells drilled after April 1, 2027. Between the payments and compound interest that accrues over time, there should be enough money available to fund the eventual cleanup of a typical well, Brian Jean, minister of energy and minerals, told a news conference Wednesday. “We are making sure that when these wells are drilled, we have something set aside for them to be cleaned up so that the taxpayers are not on the hook.” Managing the backlog of old oil and gas wells that have no one legally responsible for them, due to bankruptcy and other factors, has been a long-running issue in Alberta. Farmers have raised concern about contamination from inactive wells on their land. Cleanup of such sites is managed through the non-profit Orphan Well Association and is funded through an industry fee, the amount of which the Alberta Energy Regulator recommends to the Alberta government every year. That fee would continue to exist. The Orphan Well Levy for the 2026-27 fiscal year is $154.56 million, up from $144.45 million the previous year, though the well association has pegged total cleanup costs of its inventory at $1.66 billion. The latest monthly numbers from the Orphan Well Association say there are 7,328 wells are waiting to be decommissioned, which involves permanently dismantling equipment so that the site is safe. Another 9,258 sites are in need of reclamation, which means restoring the land so it’s similar to its original state. In the 2025-26 fiscal year, the average cost of decommissioning a well was $28,800 and for reclaiming a site, it was $27,700. Under the new rules — proposed as part of a broader bill that also includes new restrictions for data centres, greater illegal dumping fines and other matters — a company would be eligible to receive the funds that were set aside once reclamation is complete. If the well becomes orphaned, the funding would be transferred to the Orphan Well Association. “We’re making good on a promise that we made to Albertans to stop the flow of unfunded wells to the Orphan Well Association,” Jean said. “After these changes are put into effect, no new oil and gas well will end up at the OWA without industry-paid-for closure funding.” Terry Schmidtke, who chairs the Alberta Small Producers Group, said the changes will give junior oil and gas companies greater confidence to buy and sell producing wells that are drilled after the rules take effect. “By ensuring cleanup funding stays with each well when ownership changes, smaller producers can continue to invest and grow while meeting their long-term cleanup obligations and keeping Albertans employed in the industry right across the province,” Schmidtke said in the province’s news release. Farmers have long demanded greater assurances that oil and gas sites on their land will be properly cleaned up, Peter Dobbie, a property rights advocate, said in the provincial release. “These changes should ensure that any new wells drilled will be cleaned up and returned to full agricultural use when they stop producing.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026. Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

item.title: Carney striking trade deals at ‘lightning speed’ amid diversification push: expert
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney is moving fast to secure new trade deals as his government attempts to make Canada less dependent on the U.S., but there’s reason to be optimistic that an agreement between ...
item.dc:creator: Jordan Fleguel
item.content:encoded: Prime Minister Mark Carney is moving fast to secure new trade deals as his government attempts to make Canada less dependent on the U.S., but there’s reason to be optimistic that an agreement between Ottawa and Washington could come soon, an expert says. “Canada has successfully concluded several free trade agreements with our Association of Southeast Asian Nations counterparts and with the Philippines at kind of a lightning speed,” Margaret Kim, international trade counsel at Gowling WLG, told BNN Bloomberg Wednesday. “These are all part of Canada’s efforts to diversify trade away from the United States given the increasing complexity of our trade relations.” Kim’s comments came on the same day Carney met with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, where the two leaders “discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement,” according to a post-meeting readout. While trade negotiations with the U.S. remain top of mind for Carney’s government, he’s also been focused on building Canada’s economic relationship with China, the world’s second largest economy. Carney’s trip began with an announcement that Canada would drop some restrictions on imports of Chinese steel and aluminum in exchange for greater market access for Canadian pork, seafood and other agricultural products. “I think overall the tariff relief is a positive development for sure, especially for those in the pork and seafood industry,” said Kim. “We will see how this renewed sense of economic co-operation between Canada and China further develops… from a legal perspective we have to be mindful that these are provisional arrangements short of a full-fledged free trade agreement, which would give us and businesses more certainty.” Kim said Canada and China have signalled that “this is the first of many further discussions to be had,” which will likely include talks related to the sale of Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) in Canada. “I think in the area of EVs, certainly China is interested in bringing more China-manufactured EVs into the Canadian market,” she said. “But from the Canadian perspective, I think prime minister Carney has clearly stated that it has to be within the terms that are acceptable within the realities of the Canada–United States–Mexico Agreement (CUSMA).” ‘Stay optimistic’ The future of CUSMA and the broader trading relationship between Canada and the U.S. remains uncertain, as the two neighbours have yet to strike a new deal that would end a monthslong trade war. Kim said despite the diplomatic tensions and industry-specific tariffs and counter tariffs currently in place, she doesn’t see CUSMA “going anywhere,” but added that “certainly, there will be different versions of it.” Much of the negotiations between the Carney and Trump governments have taken place behind the scenes, Kim noted, saying that the two leaders meeting face to face on Wednesday is a good sign. “I think we have to stay optimistic,” she said, “and see how it shakes out.” With files from CTV News’ Graham Richardson and The Canadian Press
